title: Officer charged after woman's death
article: The Mountie driving the police cruiser that flipped on the South Klondike Highway last fall, killing the female prisoner in the back seat, is being charged under the Motor Vehicles Act.
Const. Jeff Monkman, 28, will make his first court appearance April 7 on a charge of driving without due care and attention.
The Mountie with a little more than six years in the national police force was charged Monday and issued a summons for court.
The maximum penalty is a $500-fine and/or six months' jail.
Monkman was transferred from the Carcross RCMP detachment in the fall after the crash that killed 37-year-old Heather Lynn Benson on impact. The constable wasn't injured, police said at the time.
After the crash, Monkman was evaluated and cleared for duty. He's currently a uniformed general duty officer at the Whitehorse detachment.

One of the M-Division major crimes plainclothes investigators has been in contact with Benson's family since the Sept. 27 crash. That officer has notified her family about the charge, Sgt. Guy Rook, the Yukon RCMP spokesman, told a news conference held Tuesday afternoon to announce the driving charge.
"We the Royal Canadian Mounted Police regret the circumstances that led to the death of Heather Lynn Benson and we offer our condolences to Miss Benson's family for their loss," said Rook.
"The RCMP is taking this matter very seriously," Rook said, noting an "extensive" investigation by the M-Division major crimes unit and an RCMP collision reconstruction expert.
Senior management within the Yukon RCMP kept an eye on the investigation and an Outside Mountie conducted an independent review, said Rook.
The evidence was sent to an Outside prosecutor to recommend whether charges were warranted.
As well, the Yukon coroner will hold a public inquest into Benson's death once the court proceedings are done.
Holding a coroner's inquest is standard after a person dies in custody.
The RCMP has its own disciplinary process for officers who break the law or force policy, but Rook wouldn't comment on whether Monkman has been under an internal review or if he's been disciplined.
Rook would not say if the constable underwent counselling after the prisoner in his custody died.
The Tagish woman was arrested hours before her death Sept. 27 on drug charges after police executed a search warrant. She was then taken to the Carcross detachment.

Monkman transferred Benson in a police car into Whitehorse for court, usually set for 10 a.m. on weekends. At about 5:45 a.m., his police car left the road approximately 20 kilometres south of the Carcross cutoff and rolled.
Benson was pronounced dead at the scene.
Rook said he couldn't provide any further details about the crash as it would jeopardize the court proceedings.
He wouldn't say how long Monkman had been working that night.
Benson was handcuffed with her hands in front of her when she died, said Rook, but she wasn't shackled to the inside of the vehicle.

"(RCMP) policy states that a prisoner must not be shackled to any part of the vehicle or other conveyance while it is in motion unless extraordinary circumstances exist," said Rook, reading from the national police force's written guidelines.
Handcuffing prisoners before putting them in the back seat of a police cruiser is common practice, Rook said.
Benson also wasn't wearing a seatbelt. Each police officer transporting a prisoner has to decide for himself whether it's safe to reach into the back of the car to buckle up a prisoner.

"When escorting a person in custody, the onus is on the police officer to strike a balance between ensuring their personal safety while ensuring the safety of the person in transport," Rook told reporters.
"To do this, the RCMP policy allows a police officer to exercise their judgment and discretion in ensuring a safe escort based on the circumstances in each case."
